description: Mi nombre es Ángel, estudiante de ingeniería en sistemas y tecnologías de la información, me gusta programar, hacer interfaces interactivas y siempre me ha intrigado el espacio, por eso para este hackathon me he comprometido a ayudar al ser humano a expandir sus horizontes, ayudando a los astronautas a recorrer y explorar marte con un mapa de manera segura.
summary:
The "Mapeo Marciano" project acts as an interactive web simulator, offering 2D or 3D visuals for navigating and managing routes across the Red Planet. Its client-server interaction helps to process telemetry and maps for automatically calculating or projecting safe paths.

Operations for this program rely on data analyzed from official instruments plus earlier NASA missions.

A fast asynchronous backend was built in Python using the FastAPI framework which is responsible for parsing and normalizing every catalog provided.

It uses a heuristic plus weighted version of the A-Star search algorithm that evaluates critical factors in real time like topographic slopes, heat radiation anomalies, or dust storm density to penalize nodes and plotting the best route by avoiding those hazards.

Visualization is built through the Three js library which project three-dimensional models, dynamic lighting, and particles. Such separation of functions ensures stable visuals while the server handles heavy math load and cross-origin security policies.

The technical feasibility of complex geospatial analysis combined with an accessible interface provide a scalable foundation to improve support for future planetary explorations.
details:
¿cómo funciona?

La arquitectura del proyecto Mapa Marciano se basa en un estricto modelo cliente-servidor y se apoya en la Separación de Responsabilidades. Dado que procesar mallas con millones de vértices o calcular rutas a través de matrices complejas requiere una potencia informática sustancial, hacer que el navegador del usuario ejecute todo el código provocaría desbordamientos de memoria o picos irregulares en la velocidad de fotogramas. Por este motivo, el sistema se divide principalmente en tres capas:

Capa del servidor: El backend funciona como núcleo del simulador y está integrado en Python 3.13. Aprovecha las capacidades de Python para cálculos matriciales y análisis de datos, y está organizado utilizando el marco FastAPI. Esta elección aborda la necesidad de crear puntos finales asincrónicos, lo que se vuelve esencial tan pronto como el servidor comienza a trabajar con archivos más grandes. El backend está organizado en módulos:

  • Módulo de ingestión: incluye scripts como lector_pds.py y malla_hd.py, dedicados a extraer metadatos de los catálogos oficiales de la NASA y normalizar variables físicas como la altitud y las coordenadas cartesianas.
  • Motor lógico: alberga la física y las reglas del sistema. Archivos como rutas.py y telemetria.py ejecutan la lógica matemática, integrando condiciones climáticas dinámicas en los cálculos de costos del algoritmo de navegación.
  • Capa de seguridad y enrutamiento: Este módulo gestiona políticas de intercambio de recursos, lo que permite que el frontend consuma datos del servidor sin ser bloqueado por las medidas de seguridad del navegador.

Client layer: visual presentation and user interaction are handled by the web client, which maintains lightweight analytical logic to avoid overloading the browser, although its rendering pipeline is sophisticated because it is built using HTML5 standards and advanced CSS, and is further enhanced by Three.js, a graphics library based on WebGL.

The JavaScript modules sequence the visual rendering process. As soon as the client receives the data structure from the server, Three.js incorporates the altitude coordinates along the Z-axis to generate a topographically accurate three-dimensional mesh. The engine then applies displacement maps, textures, particle systems (emulating dust storms), and dynamic shading, ensuring a smooth user experience without drops in the frame rate.

Communication protocol: a file obtained from the NASA Mars Trek database enters the backend through a module called ingesta.py, which processes more than thirty file types, such as .tif, .jpg, and .png, to begin processing and building the map. After being processed, the file passes through FastAPI, which communicates with Three.js to ultimately produce a two-dimensional and three-dimensional graphic.

To plot optimal routes across the surface of Mars, a weighted variant of the A* (A-Star) algorithm was implemented. It not only evaluates the shortest distance between points, but also takes into account multiple variables that the program interprets as environmental and physical risks.

The system implements a weighted impact model in which each transition between adjacent nodes is multiplied by a dynamic penalty factor based on terrain and atmospheric conditions. If a node presents adverse conditions, its computational impact increases exponentially, forcing the algorithm to discard it and continue along another route.

 

What Benefits Does It have?

Our web application offers several benefits, such as 3D web visualization, which makes it possible to view a 3D version of the map at a stable 60 frames per second thanks to the system's high level of optimization. It also offers a product capable of plotting routes and modifying them in real time depending on the current hazards on the surface of Mars. In addition, because our web application is client-side, we can access it independently without needing an internet connection.

A real-time interaction system that allows the user to take control of a tornado and move freely around the map.

 

What Is the Project's Expected Impact?

We believe our project offers many opportunities for further development, such as future implementations of our system on smartwatches, further enhanced with AI to keep astronauts in the best possible condition; support for space robots such as the Rover in making critical decisions to prevent future damage that could render the robots unusable; and the development of Mars' cartography through the discovery of new areas as exploration progresses, among other possibilities. Furthermore, with the possibility of receiving support from NASA for this project, it could be further enhanced and brought to a much more realistic scale, making fully digital simulations possible. It could even be possible to extend this work from Mars to other planets that may be explored.

 

What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software were used to develop your project?

The project was developed and refined using Gemini Argon and Claude Opus 5.5 AI, along with GitHub skills.

The first step was taken with Argon, which was used to plan the product by developing a simple map matrix and a 3D plane that would serve as the basis for the project's development. It was mainly replaced because it could not keep up with the processes we were carrying out, since it could not run tests autonomously and the code would often become fragmented halfway through an execution. Then, thanks to Argon together with Claude, we were able to expand the graphics engine's processing capabilities and its ability to resolve tasks, as well as improve the map's quality and accuracy (higher resolution) and, additionally, develop and implement new tools.

Thanks to Claude Opus 5.5 and the skills obtained from GitHub, we were able to further develop the HTML, JavaScript, and Python programming, expanding the program's capabilities and the tasks it can perform, as well as optimizing it so that it could support 3D maps despite not having a dedicated graphics card. In addition, we enabled Claude to analyze vulnerabilities and glitches on the website so they could be fixed and the system hardened, thereby optimizing the system and making it more secure for the future.

 

In What Way Is Your Project Creative?

We looked for ways to make the project innovative by addressing aspects that have not been addressed so far, or for which solutions are not easy to find. In addition, thanks to the wide range of opportunities it offers, we can further develop the application in the future to solve more complex problems that, although they are not part of the main problem, our project may help address.

 

What Factors Did Your Team Take into Account?

To prioritize the explorer's safety, we mainly considered that the user should play a role in assisting with decision-making in order to complete the mission as quickly and safely as possible.

The next consideration is to use the program to safeguard exploration probes, enabling them to operate autonomously offline if the system disconnects, in order to prioritize the probe's safety.

In both cases, the system predicts disturbances or changes on the surface caused by dynamic weather conditions, interpreting them within the mathematical logic as danger zones in order to avoid plotting routes across any of these disturbances.

The program helps users analyze the surfaces by overlaying, in layers, the various radiation, temperature, and atmospheric pressure impacts from the queried database, which makes it possible to justify routes and safe areas for avoiding meteorological events.

To prevent the program from becoming overloaded, it filters the information, processing, and visualization of datasets from NASA's PDS (Planetary Data System) through the ingestion modules, the logic module, and the graphics engine.
